evidence: The introduction promises revenue, variable-cost, attribution, and assumption boundaries; the six sections then cover model boundary, revenue basis, cost boundary, attribution, examples/rounding, and source review policy.
The conclusion routes readers to tools and guides only after defining how ROAS Break turns contribution into break-even and target thresholds.

Shopify sales fields and GA4 ecommerce fields are linked as official sources, while the page labels its revenue treatment as the default recommendation and its calculators as decision models rather than accounting statements.
The attribution section explicitly limits platform-reported ROAS and states that the calculators do not prove incrementality or promise delivery.
The page contains no numeric worked scenario to recalculate; its three displayed identities were checked dimensionally: C=R-V, break-even ROAS=R/C, and target ROAS=R/(C-P).
The rounding section is internally consistent with the stated two-decimal money/ratio and one-decimal percentage display policy.
The page connects contribution margin, break-even ROAS, target CPA, realized POAS, period MER, and cohort CAC payback using one named revenue and cost basis.
Separate order, store, and customer sections explain why units and populations cannot be substituted, directly satisfying the declared connection intent.

The sources section attributes report fields and ROAS definitions to Shopify and Amazon, then explicitly labels contribution, POAS, allowable CPA, and payback relationships as ROAS Break modeling choices.
The model-limit note separates calculation outputs from incrementality, delivery forecasts, accounting definitions, cash timing, and benchmarks.
Order example recomputed: 40+8+4+3+5=60; 100-60=40; margin=40%; break-even ROAS=100/40=2.50; retained target=10; allowable CPA=30; target ROAS=100/30=3.33.
Actual result recomputed: CPA 25 gives ROAS 100/25=4.00, after-ad contribution 40-25=15, and POAS 15/25=0.60.
Period and cohort extensions recomputed: 100000-60000-25000=15000, MER=100000/25000=4.00, claimed ratio=110000/25000=4.40, CAC=25000/600=41.67, day-90 payback, and allowable day-365 CAC=72-15=57.
The direct answer defines revenue ROAS and the page-specific after-ad contribution POAS boundary, then the metric table and operating sections explain when contribution profit is more useful.
MER, incrementality, fixed overhead, attribution, and volume limits prevent the comparison from collapsing into a single ratio recommendation.

The sources section assigns Amazon ROAS and Shopify report fields to official documentation and explicitly calls the POAS numerator, assumptions, and incrementality advice ROAS Break modeling choices.
The page states that its POAS definition is not universal and labels the example as neither a benchmark, forecast, nor causal estimate.
Base case recomputed: 45+8+3+3+5=64; contribution=100-64=36; spend=100/4=25; after-ad contribution=11; POAS=11/25=0.44.
Sensitivity cases recomputed: at 2.50x spend=40, result=-4 and POAS=-4/40=-0.10; at 5.00x spend=20, result=16 and POAS=16/20=0.80.
The direct answer distinguishes gross from contribution margin and states why contribution, not gross margin, sets the acquisition ceiling.
The cost-coverage table, margin-versus-markup warning, complete order example, and input workflow support the declared choice intent.
Shopify profit and sales definitions are linked as sources; cost inclusion, cohort maturity, and segmentation language is presented as a modeling workflow rather than attributed to Shopify.
The decision-boundary note explicitly excludes fixed overhead and directs readers to reserve it deliberately instead of presenting the boundary as universal accounting.
Partial view recomputed: 120-48=72, gross margin=72/120=60%, break-even ROAS=1/0.60=1.67; the $60-on-$100 margin/markup example gives 40% margin and 66.7% markup.
Full view recomputed: 120-48-9-3.60-9.60=49.80, contribution margin=41.5%, break-even ROAS=120/49.80=2.41, and the unrounded partial allowance 72 exceeds the full allowance by 22.20.
The direct answer recommends a consistent net product revenue basis, while the field map explains how gross sales, net sales, total sales, tax, shipping, platform value, and losses differ.
The reconciliation and workflow show how to choose and preserve one numerator before comparing ROAS, directly satisfying the declared intent.
The page explicitly labels net product revenue as ROAS Break's decision-model default rather than a universal accounting standard.
Shopify sales definitions and GA4 purchase/refund fields are cited separately from the page's recommendations about tax, shipping, maturity, and reconciliation.
Revenue reconciliation recomputed: gross product sales 100 minus discount 10 and mature return 5 equals net product revenue 85; tax 8 is excluded and shipping 6 is tracked separately.
Contribution recomputed: fee=3% of 85=2.55; 85-30-8-3-2.55=41.45; break-even ROAS=85/41.45=2.05.
The page maps Shopify net sales, orders, COGS, shipping, taxes, fees, fulfillment, and return handling into the calculator's order-level inputs.
The worked report and missing-cost checklist turn that mapping into a break-even ROAS workflow, matching the declared primary intent.
The page says 'For the ROAS Break model' before recommending net sales per order and links official Shopify sales and profit reports for the field definitions.
Warnings about maturity, missing costs, tax, shipping, and double-counting are visibly framed as model checks rather than Shopify guarantees.
Net sales recomputed: 100-10-5=85; fee=0.03*85=2.55; contribution=85-30-8-3-2.55=41.45; break-even ROAS=85/41.45=2.05.
At 2.40x, CPA=85/2.40=35.42 and after-ad contribution=41.45-35.4167=6.03, matching the displayed result.
The converter, reciprocal table, and formulas explain both ROAS-to-ACoS directions, then the profit-threshold section connects both ratios to available contribution.
The Amazon cost checklist prevents the conversion from being mistaken for a profitability target, satisfying the full declared intent.
The page attributes ACoS and ROAS definitions to two Amazon Ads sources, then separately states that seller economics require a product-specific contribution model.
Advice about complete costs, reporting windows, and what counts as a good ACoS is framed as decision guidance rather than an Amazon rule.
Every reciprocal table row recomputes with ACoS%=100/ROAS: 1.25->80%, 2.00->50%, 2.50->40%, 4.00->25%, and 5.00->20%.
Profit target recomputed: 40% contribution gives 2.50x break-even; retaining 10% leaves 30% ACoS and target ROAS=100/30=3.33.
The page rejects a universal good ROAS and derives a target from store contribution, retained profit, revenue basis, maturity, and useful volume.
Three margin scenarios and the operating checklist demonstrate how the store's own cost structure changes its threshold.
Amazon ROAS and Shopify profit-report context are sourced, while the page explicitly identifies the target method and scenarios as ROAS Break modeling choices.
The examples are labeled illustrative and not sector averages; the delivery and volume tradeoff is stated as a model limit.
For 75% margin: contribution=75-3-5=67, break-even=100/67=1.49, target=100/(67-15)=1.92.
For 55% margin: contribution=47, break-even=100/47=2.13, target=100/32=3.13; for 40% margin: contribution=32, break-even=3.13, target=100/17=5.88.
The direct answer derives allowable ad spend from contribution and retained profit, converts the ratio to Google's percentage format, and distinguishes the business floor from the bidding input.
The conversion-value boundary and operational checks explain how to apply the threshold without treating it as a delivery promise.
Google target ROAS bidding and conversion adjustments are linked to official documentation; the page explicitly calls retained-profit conversion ROAS Break's model, not a Google recommendation.
The warning that a 286% bid target does not promise realized ROAS or volume keeps platform behavior separate from business advice.
Contribution recomputed from a 100 order: gross profit 58 minus fees 3 and returns allowance 5 equals 50; break-even ROAS=100/50=2.00.
Retaining 15 leaves target CPA 35; target ROAS=100/35=2.857, displayed as 2.86x and 286% after conversion and rounding.

The direct answer maps one Meta ad set's attributed purchase value and recorded attribution settings into separate contribution break-even and retained-profit thresholds, matching the declared primary intent.

The reporting contract captures ad set, event, model/settings, value basis, dates, timezone, and currency; the boundary explicitly excludes channel-claim aggregation and store-wide MER, leaving that reconciliation to the distinct attributed-roas-vs-mer guide.

Both Meta Business Help Center links returned HTTP 200 with the expected attribution-settings and attribution-system titles; their responses contain substantial JavaScript and serialized page content, supporting the guide's cautious statement that the full public body can depend on JavaScript.

The guide attributes reporting controls and concepts to Meta, labels contribution math and the 2.63x/3.57x thresholds as ROAS Break modeling rather than Meta recommendations, and avoids asserting a universal default attribution window.

Account- and campaign-specific option availability cannot be established from a public page alone; the guide states this evidence limit and requires the actual selected account/ad-set settings as the operational source of truth.
Reported Meta ROAS recomputed as 32000/10000=3.20x; per-order contribution is 100-42-8-4-3-5=38, so the 38% contribution floor is 100/38=2.63x.
Retaining 10 leaves target CPA 38-10=28 and target ROAS 100/28=3.57x; at 3.20x the ad cost per credited order is 100/3.20=31.25 and modeled after-ad contribution is 38-31.25=6.75.
The stated conclusion is correct: 3.20x exceeds the 2.63x zero-profit floor but remains below 3.57x and retains 6.75 rather than the planned 10.
The formulas calculate break-even and target ACoS directly from contribution and retained profit, then convert both to ROAS.
The worked seller scenario and fee checklist show the product-specific costs needed to use the thresholds, matching the declared Amazon acquisition intent.
Amazon Ads ACoS and ROAS definitions are cited as official facts; the seller cost boundary and retained-profit target are explicitly labeled ROAS Break modeling choices.
The 15% marketplace fee is labeled an input rather than a universal Amazon category benchmark.
Fee and contribution recomputed: 15% of 60=9; 60-18-8-4-9=21; cost shares are 30%, 13.3%, 6.7%, and 15%, leaving 35% contribution.
Break-even ACoS=21/60=35% and ROAS=1/0.35=2.86; reserving 6 leaves 15 for ads, so target ACoS=25% and ROAS=4.00.

The direct answer rebuilds regular, one-unit discount, and two-unit bundle orders from full revenue, COGS, fulfillment, fee, return, and other-cost ledgers before comparing them at the same traffic and order reference.
Same-traffic, same-order, same-unit, same-customer, return-window, and acquisition-basis sections expose the denominator and resource tradeoffs, directly satisfying the declared comparison intent.

Shopify discount types, bundle mechanics, and profit-report context are linked as platform facts; the order-cost ledger, fictional calculations, normalization rules, and thresholds are explicitly labeled ROAS Break modeling judgments.
The page labels the example fictional and states that neither bundle conversion nor incremental demand, customer value, or net income is forecast or guaranteed.

At 100 orders totals are 3660, 2188, and 5176; changes versus regular are -1472 and +1516, the bundle exceeds the direct discount by 2988, and 50 bundle orders on 100 units produce 2588, which is 400 above direct and 1072 below regular.
Thresholds recomputed: 3660/21.88=167.3 orders and 4.18% CVR (+67.3%); 3660/51.76=70.7 bundle orders and 1.77% CVR (-29.3%), consuming 141.4 units at the unrounded threshold.
The direct answer separates customer shipping revenue from merchant fulfillment cost and derives order-lift, CVR, and merchandise-AOV thresholds on one contribution basis.

The fixed-cost boundary, incremental-basket example, and contribution-per-visitor readout explain when each threshold is valid and how to test it, matching the declared AOV/order/conversion-lift intent.

Shopify free-shipping controls, shipping-charge reporting, and profit-report fields are linked as official context; the contribution boundary, thresholds, and experiment recommendations are explicitly labeled ROAS Break modeling judgments.
The page labels the scenario fictional, holds tax and advertising outside the model, and distinguishes controlled-test evidence from observational before/after changes.
Regular contribution recomputed: 86-32-8-4-(8%*86)=35.12; free-shipping contribution=80-32-8-4-(8%*80)=29.60; the loss is 5.52 because percentage costs fall by 0.48.
Volume thresholds recomputed: 35.12/29.60-1=18.6%, about 119 orders per 100; 2.50%*35.12/29.60=2.97%, a 0.47-point or 18.6% relative CVR lift.
AOV thresholds recomputed: (35.12+32+8+4)/(1-3%-5%)=86.00, 7.5% above 80; adding 2 COGS and 1 fulfillment gives (35.12+34+9+4)/0.92=89.26.
The page separately defines discount, refund, restockable return, unsellable return, and cancellation mechanisms and assigns each a different operating response.
The corrected worked return and promotion workflow show why return-rate percentages and discount economics require different models, satisfying the separation intent.
Shopify sales adjustments and GA4 purchase/refund fields are linked as official source context; the expected-loss equation and possible actions are visibly presented as the page's modeling workflow.
The page states that return rate does not automatically equal a loss allowance and exposes product recovery and operational costs as assumptions.
After correction 4575903, original contribution is 100-35-3=62; a restockable return loses 62 contribution plus 3 retained fee plus 9 reverse logistics, totaling 74 versus keeping the sale.
An unsellable return adds 35 inventory loss, so total impact is 74+35=109; an 8% to 10% rate change is 2 percentage points and 2/8=25% relative.

The direct answer prevents revenue LTV from becoming allowable CAC by defining fixed-window revenue LTV, contribution LTV before acquisition, and allowable CAC with the original acquired-customer denominator.
The order-level cost boundary, interval ledger, fixed-window table, maturity rules, and payback conclusion carry the declared contribution-versus-revenue intent through 30/60/90/180/365 days.

Shopify customer, sales, and profit reports plus GA4 purchase/refund fields are linked as external reporting facts; fixed checkpoints, contribution boundaries, fictional order history, retained-profit policy, and allowable-CAC math are explicitly labeled ROAS Break modeling judgments.
The page labels repeat counts fictional observations rather than forecasts, refuses to call a 365-day observation lifetime value, and separates contribution payback from cash payback and net income.

Per-order and interval ledgers recomputed: variable cost=40+8+3+5+4=60 and contribution=40; 100/30/20/35/45 orders produce revenue 10000/3000/2000/3500/4500, costs 6000/1800/1200/2100/2700, and contribution 4000/1200/800/1400/1800.

Using the original 100-customer denominator, cumulative orders are 100/130/150/185/230, Revenue LTV is 100/130/150/185/230, repeat contribution is 0/12/20/34/52, and Contribution LTV is 40/52/60/74/92 at days 30/60/90/180/365.

Actual CAC 70 is not covered at 40, 52, or 60 and first pays back at day 180 where 74 leaves 4; day-365 allowable CAC=92-15=77, while actual CAC leaves 92-70=22 and 22-15=7 beyond the retained target.
The direct answer defines separate new-customer, cohort, and blended-store denominators and formulas rather than assigning one common threshold.
Identity controls, payback-window rules, and the three-boundary table explain how to set and govern distinct acquisition and store-wide profitability thresholds.

Google Ads new-customer controls and Shopify customer reporting are tied to official sources; the reconciliation order, contribution boundary, fictional calculations, and CAC policy are explicitly labeled modeling judgments.
The example is labeled fictional, and platform new-customer labels are separated from the finance-approved ledger definition without dismissing their optimization use.
Period results recomputed: blended ROAS=100000/20000=5.00; target=1/(45%-10%)=2.86; new-customer ROAS=25000/20000=1.25; CAC=20000/250=80.
First-order results recomputed: revenue per customer=100, contribution=(25000-15000)/250=40, break-even ROAS=100/40=2.50, and 75000 of store revenue lies outside verified first orders.
Cohort results recomputed: checkpoints 40/55/68 remain below CAC 80 until day 180 at 90; day-365 allowable CAC=112-12=100.
The page defines cumulative contribution and first mature payback checkpoint, then gives a six-step cohort preparation workflow aligned to customer identity, dates, revenue, costs, and spend.
The worked cohort, input-shape warning, and data limits show how to prepare mature 30/60/90/180/365-day values without calling them lifetime value.
GA4 purchase/refund fields and Shopify customer-report context are linked as source inputs; the contribution boundary, checkpoint policy, and allowable-CAC rule are presented as the page's method.
The page explicitly refuses unobserved extrapolation and labels the exact observation window rather than treating platform or revenue data as a universal LTV claim.
Against CAC 70, cumulative contribution leaves gaps of 25 at day 30 and 8 at day 60, then exceeds CAC by 6 at day 90, 22 at day 180, and 48 at day 365.
The first checkpoint at or above 70 is day 90, and allowable day-365 CAC with retained profit 15 is 118-15=103.

The page normalizes CTA-only, CTA+VTA, Assisted gross revenue (Shop), and store net revenue as separately labeled replacement numerators under one contribution formula, directly satisfying the declared comparison intent.

Its boundary leaves cross-channel overlap and store-wide MER reconciliation to the distinct attributed-roas-vs-mer guide, while this page focuses on TikTok settings, windows, revenue meanings, and financial normalization.

The workflow explicitly prohibits summing the four views or calling attribution incremental without a causal design, and requires event, window, value basis, timezone, currency, and extraction-time labels.

TikTok Ads Manager Help directly defines Assisted gross revenue (Shop) as gross revenue from people exposed to ads within 28 days before purchase and also documents attribution metrics including VTA; both official URLs returned HTTP 200 during review.

The TikTok for Business article separately contains Performance Comparison and Time to Conversion analysis; after correction a1c566d, the guide no longer uses that blog as evidence for Assisted Shop or the 28-day exposure period.

The page limits the 28-day statement to Assisted Shop, requires the configured CTA/VTA windows for exact reports, labels feature availability as variable, and identifies the 40% margin and fictional scenarios as ROAS Break assumptions rather than TikTok profit claims.
With spend 10000 and AOV 50, CTA-only gives revenue=2.50*10000=25000, orders=25000/50=500, and contribution profit=25000*40%-10000=0.
CTA+VTA gives revenue=3.20*10000=32000, orders=640, and contribution profit=32000*40%-10000=2800; store net at 2.70x gives revenue=27000, orders=540, and contribution profit=800.

Changing store net to 3.50x gives revenue=35000, orders=35000/50=700, and contribution profit=35000*40%-10000=4000; the page correctly treats this as a changed scenario input rather than a prediction.
The three-view table distinguishes platform-attributed ROAS, store-total MER, and contribution profit, then the reconciliation workflow keeps windows, spend, and revenue definitions separate.
The overlapping-credit example directly demonstrates how channel claims reconcile to a smaller store total without manufacturing revenue.

Shopify marketing reporting and attribution context is cited as the external fact source; the recommendation to keep platform credit, store revenue, and contribution profit separate is explicitly labeled a ROAS Break modeling judgment.
The boundary note states that neither MER nor attributed ROAS proves profit or causality.
Store MER recomputed as 100000/25000=4.00; Google ratio=55000/12000=4.58 and Meta ratio=65000/13000=5.00.
Platform credit sums to 120000 while spend sums to 25000, leaving 20000 more credited revenue than the 100000 store total; the page correctly refuses to treat that overlap as sales.
The page answers when recent attributed ROAS is mature enough for budget decisions by separating observed T+1 and T+7 results from an explicitly hypothetical conversion-maturity sensitivity curve.

Its decision gate uses the maturity estimate only to judge data readiness, while the linked target-ROAS guidance supplies the separate economic threshold; this division matches the declared primary intent.

Google's official conversion-lag page returned HTTP 200 and explains that conversions can be reported after the ad interaction; Google's official Target ROAS page also returned HTTP 200 and defines Target ROAS bidding.

The guide labels the 70%, 90%, and T+7 maturity curve as fictional sensitivity inputs rather than a Google benchmark, forecast, or booked revenue, and labels the cost model and decision gates as ROAS Break judgments.
T+1 recomputed: reported ROAS=20000/10000=2.00x; at 70% sensitivity, estimated mature revenue=20000/0.70=28571.43, mature ROAS=2.86x, and remaining sensitivity=8571.43.
T+7 recomputed: reported ROAS=27000/10000=2.70x. Unit economics give contribution=100-40-8-4-3-5=40, break-even ROAS=100/40=2.50x, retained profit=10, target CPA=30, and target ROAS=100/30=3.33x.
At 2.70x, ad cost per credited order=100/2.70=37.04 and modeled after-ad contribution=40-37.04=2.96, correctly above break-even but below the retained-profit target.

The page carries its declared intent from transaction correction through matched-spend ROAS recalculation: Google Ads retractions/restatements and GA4 refunds feed an idempotent adjustment ledger, processing wait, and store-control reconciliation.

Its scope is distinct from the linked guides: returns-and-discounts models economic loss, ecommerce-revenue-basis chooses the numerator, and google-ads-target-roas-profit supplies the business threshold after values mature.

Google Ads Help confirms that RESTATEMENT changes conversion value without changing conversion count, while RETRACTION changes value to zero, removes the conversion from the count, and prevents further adjustment; the API reference uses adjusted_value for RESTATEMENT.

The GA4 refund reference requires transaction_id, recommends item information for item-level refund metrics, and defines item quantity; the Data API defines purchaseRevenue as purchase revenue minus refunded transaction revenue, supporting the guide's no-double-subtraction warning.

The platform write-back rules are attributed to official Google sources, while the fictional cohort, 40% contribution assumption, idempotent control ledger, unresolved-gap queue, and decision sequence are explicitly presented as ROAS Break modeling and operating judgments.
Initial attributed ROAS recomputes as 40000/10000=4.00x; subtracting 5000 of retracted value and 1000 of aggregate restatement reductions leaves 34000 and 34000/10000=3.40x.
The 33000 store control is 1000 below adjusted Ads value and gives 3.30x. At 40% contribution margin, after-ad contribution is 40000*40%-10000=6000, 34000*40%-10000=3600, and 33000*40%-10000=3200.
The displayed 400, 340, and 330 orders equal each scenario's revenue divided by the planner's 100 AOV and are correctly labeled normalization only, not Google Ads conversion counts.

The page directly fulfills its declared intent by holding ad spend equal, deriving revenue and normalized orders from each scenario's ROAS and AOV, and ranking product-channel combinations by total contribution after advertising rather than ROAS alone.

Its role remains distinct from related assets: poas-vs-roas defines the profit ratio, attributed-roas-vs-mer reconciles channel credit with store totals, shopify-net-sales-for-roas maps commerce report inputs, and ecommerce-profit-formulas connects the general metric relationships; this guide applies already-defined inputs to scenario ranking.

All four official sources returned HTTP 200: GA4 documents ecommerce transaction, item, purchase, refund, metric, and dimension fields; Shopify defines InventoryItem unitCost as the unit cost associated with the inventory item; Amazon defines ROAS as campaign revenue divided by campaign spend.

The guide explicitly limits Shopify unitCost to merchandise-cost mapping and requires fulfillment, payment, marketplace, return, duty, packaging, incentive, and other variable costs before calling the result contribution margin.

The fictional AOV, margins, ROAS values, equal-spend control, and ranking are labeled ROAS Break assumptions; attribution is separated from causality and overlapping channel credit, while the scale warning rejects linear extrapolation when auctions, mix, inventory, or costs change.
At 10000 spend, the 50 AOV, 20% margin, 5.00x scenario gives revenue=50000, normalized orders=50000/50=1000, and contribution after ads=50000*20%-10000=0.

The 80 AOV, 40% margin, 4.00x scenario gives revenue=40000, orders=500, and contribution=6000; the 100 AOV, 55% margin, 3.00x scenario gives revenue=30000, orders=300, and contribution=6500, correctly winning by 500 over Balanced and 6500 over High ROAS.

When the high-margin scenario falls to 2.80x, revenue=28000, normalized orders=28000/100=280, and contribution=28000*55%-10000=5400, so Balanced remains at 6000 and becomes the winner; all displayed order counts are correctly labeled revenue/AOV normalization rather than observed transactions.

The page fulfills its unique input-audit intent by requiring source, period, currency, owner, amount, destination, and status for every pre-ad variable cost, then enforcing one destination, fixed-versus-variable, and missing-versus-zero checks before opening the calculator.

All six groups map explicitly to the calculator: revenue deductions to aov, product and inbound to cogs, fulfillment to ship, percentage payment/platform costs to fees and fixed components to other, refunded revenue to returns with reverse-logistics or unrecovered loss in other, and remaining variable service costs to other.

Its boundary is distinct from related assets: contribution-margin explains why contribution sets the acquisition ceiling, ecommerce-profit-formulas connects approved inputs to CPA/POAS/MER/payback, and methodology states the site's broader revenue, cost, attribution, and review rules.

All five official sources returned HTTP 200: GA4 documents ecommerce value, currency, discount, item, purchase, and refund fields; its Data API documents revenue and refund metrics; Shopify documents InventoryItem unitCost and Refund line items, transactions, order adjustments, and totals; Stripe documents balance-transaction amount, fee, net, currency, and reporting_category.

The guide treats platform fields as source evidence rather than a completed cost model and explicitly labels the six-group mapping, one-destination rule, contribution boundary, and fictional calculations as ROAS Break choices rather than platform accounting guidance.

The refund rule prevents deducting mature refunded revenue in both aov and returns/other, while the fixed-cost and missing-zero controls keep baseline overhead separate and require evidence for genuine zero values; tax, accounting classification, cash timing, attribution, demand, inventory, and forecasting remain outside scope.
Revenue and cost ledger recomputed: 135-15=120 aov; fees=120*3%=3.60; expected refunded revenue=120*8%=9.60; total pre-ad variable cost=48+9+7+3.60+9.60=77.20.
Contribution=120-77.20=42.80, contribution margin=42.80/120=35.6667% displayed as 35.7%, and break-even ROAS=120/42.80=2.8037x displayed as 2.80x.

The incomplete COGS-only view gives 120-48=72, 72/120=60%, and 120/72=1.67x while omitting 9+7+3.60+9.60=29.20; at 3.00x, ad cost is 120/3=40 and after-ad contribution is 2.80 per order, so 1000/40=25 orders produce 25*2.80=70.
